item.title: Researchers Develop Compositional Concept Unlearning for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
item.description:
Researchers Develop Compositional Concept Unlearning for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Researchers have introduced Compositional Concept Unlearning (C$^2$U), a method designed to address the risk of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems exposing unwanted concepts through retrieved evidence. This approach functions even when the generator itself is moderated.

🧩 How it works

C$^2$U operates using a fixed encoder and document index to perform query-side concept suppression. The process includes the following mechanisms:

  • It routes a profile-derived direction through an augmented atom bank.
  • It adds a bounded edited-minus-original delta to the raw query.
  • It suppresses target density while maintaining budgeted control-query exposure.

⚙️ Key details

The configuration’s effectiveness was evaluated across five datasets, four encoders, and three seeds. Validation results showed:

  • A 4.25 percentage point reduction in pooled binary target Hit@5.
  • No positive control degradation.
  • Observed changes in target-exposure.

Additionally, ArXiv four-concept composition showed performance improvements over an averaged-direction comparator after independent validation gates and first-use test evaluation.

#AI #MachineLearning #RAG #DataPrivacy

Source: C$^2$U in RAG: Compositional Concept Unlearning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation

item.title: State Attorneys General Push for Data Protections as Character.AI Files for Bankruptcy
item.description:
State Attorneys General Push for Data Protections as Character.AI Files for Bankruptcy

Character.AI announced on Tuesday that it is filing for Chapter 11 bankruptcy and is selling some assets to Disney. The filing triggered a multi‑state investigation led by New York Attorney General Letitia James, who, together with 39 other bipartisan attorneys general, is seeking safeguards for the company’s user data.

🔍 Overview

  • Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 and disclosed that several states were mid‑investigation when the bankruptcy filing occurred.
  • The investigation began in 2024 after a lawsuit from the mother of a 14‑year‑old who died by suicide allegedly seconds after talking with the chatbot.
  • The AGs describe the findings as “exceptionally serious dangers” and “potentially unlawful conduct.”

⚖️ Legal Actions

  • Letitia James revealed a years‑long multi‑state probe into Character.AI’s consumer‑data practices.
  • James is among 40 bipartisan AGs who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy case “to put all parties on notice of the regulatory issues that will need to be addressed in any sale or transfer of the Debtor’s business or assets.”
  • The states are urging the bankruptcy judge to require the purchaser of Character.AI’s assets to implement specific data‑protection procedures.

📊 Consumer Risks Highlighted by the Investigation

  • Highly sensitive conversations users have with chatbot characters.
  • Large number of minors using the product.
  • Chatbots posing as licensed professionals.
  • Exposure to sexual and violent content.
  • Weak age‑verification checks.
  • Misleading safety claims.
  • Potential violations of state privacy laws.

🛡️ Proposed Safeguards for Any Buyer

  • Effective age‑assurance systems.
  • Restrictions on how minors can engage with the chatbots.
  • Implementation of “Crisis safeguards.”
  • Mechanisms that let users delete their data.

The AGs warn that without such protections, “this company collected some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared, and now those conversations could be sold off to the highest bidder.” James said, “I am fighting to make sure any buyer puts children’s safety first and puts real protections in place.”

Character.AI and Disney have not responded to requests for comment.

#CharacterAI #DataPrivacy #Bankruptcy

Source: Now that Character.AI is going bankrupt, what happens to all of its users’ data?

item.title: AI Labs Buying Data from Defunct Startups as New Market Emerges
item.description:
AI Labs Buying Data from Defunct Startups as New Market Emerges

AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models, turning the end‑of‑life ecosystem into a nascent data‑resale market.

🔍 Overview

  • When crypto startup founder Keelan Miskell wound down his company, he sold the code base for about $25,000 and a pending ~$15,000 for workspace data (Google, Notion, Figma, Slack) through SimpleClosure.
  • SimpleClosure added data sales to its services in April and now runs an Asset Hub platform that lets founders sell code and workspace data such as emails, chats, and documents.
  • Buyers include foundation AI labs, vendors that build simulated workspaces for AI training, and mature tech companies building their own models.

🧩 How the Market Works

  • SimpleClosure brokered over 150 deals and expects to return > $10 million to startups by the end of 2026.
  • 47 % of SimpleClosure’s deals now include code or data sales, according to CEO Dori Yona.
  • Rival Sunset also runs a data‑resale business; its CEO Brendan Mahony values assets by head count, years in operation, data volume, and tool usage, likening the exhaust data to “particle board.”
  • Demand surged last year as AI labs hit limits of public and synthetic datasets.
  • Companies like Surge AI buy archives to build reinforcement‑learning gyms where agents practice tasks (e.g., debugging IT architecture, drafting appellate briefs). Lead Nick Heiner says a rich Slack history can be more valuable than a combination of Slack, email, and calendars.

📊 Key Statistics

Metric Figure
Annual rise in startup shutdowns 26 %–56 % (Carta & AngelList)
Deals that include code/data (SimpleClosure) 47 %
Asset Hub deals handled >150
Expected return to startups (2026) > $10 M

🤝 Notable Deals & Players

  • Google outbid Mercor for Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy data: 100 M emails, 500 M Teams messages, 176 k employee records for $10 M (August).
  • SpaceX AI unit is reportedly weighing data purchases from struggling startups (September, Bloomberg).
  • Surge AI purchases real‑world archives to avoid synthetic‑world errors; pricing varies because valuations are based on research theses about task usefulness.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Attorneys like Greg Ewing call the data “legally radioactive,” noting that even after scrubbing, private details (doctor appointments, school pickups, date‑night plans) can remain.
  • Proceeds typically flow to senior creditors and investors, not to employees.
  • Law professor Ifeoma Ajunwa describes the practice as “captured capital” and argues that employers should obtain explicit consent before selling workers’ data, though no federal law currently bans such sales.
  • Founders have little visibility into who purchases their data or how it will be used.

The emerging ecosystem—coaches, “death doulas,” legal and tax specialists—reflects a growing market for the operational exhaust of companies that are winding down.

#AIData #StartupClosure #MachineLearning #DataPrivacy

Source: AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models

item.title: OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse
item.description:
OpenAI Unveils Dots AI Agent as Privacy-Focused Alternative to Meta Muse

At this year’s OpenAI DevDay, CEO Sam Altman introduced Dots, a new AI agent designed to set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI. The announcement included direct critiques of Meta’s Muse, with OpenAI positioning its new assistant as a more secure and trustworthy alternative to its primary competitor.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI executives used the launch of Dots to highlight security concerns surrounding Meta’s Muse, which had previously launched as a safer alternative to the agent OpenClaw. While Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg promised Muse was built for privacy and security, the platform has faced scrutiny over data collection and vulnerabilities. OpenAI’s leadership, including Codex product lead Alexander Embiricos, stated the company is focused on providing the most secure assistant while avoiding the mistakes of rivals.

⚙️ Key details

AI Agent Developer Stated Privacy and Security Approach
Dots OpenAI Zero data retention policy options for enterprises and individual user-set rules.
Muse Meta User data stored in isolated Linux VMs with browser, CPU, memory, and storage.
OpenClaw (Not specified) Predecessor to Muse; described as less safe than subsequent alternatives.

🧩 Capabilities and Controls

OpenAI and Meta have implemented different strategies to manage user data and agent behavior:

  • OpenAI Dots: Users can exert individual control over the agent, such as setting rules to prevent it from making purchases over a specific dollar amount. Enterprise customers can access frameworks with stronger data controls and options to ensure no data is stored on OpenAI servers.
  • Meta Muse: The agent defaults to allowing Meta to train models on user input, though an opt-out is available. While the company plans to introduce cryptographic methods to prevent internal access to VM data, Meta currently retains access.

🚀 Availability

OpenAI has launched Dots with a focus on its high-end user base, currently making it available only on the $100-and-up ChatGPT subscription tiers. In contrast, Meta’s Muse saw rapid adoption following its release, gaining 600,000 daily active users in the United States within weeks and topping App Store charts.

💡 Why it matters

The push for more private AI agents comes as labs try to convince users to share increasingly personal information. Despite Meta’s privacy promises for Muse, security researchers exposed a zero-day vulnerability, and reports indicated the agent created detailed profiles of users’ social networks and shared private data, such as physical addresses and private messages, as part of its intended functions. OpenAI’s strategy with Dots relies on one-upping these rivals by promising stricter data boundaries, though some users still report discomfort when asked to provide sensitive financial information to these agents.

#OpenAI #Dots #Meta #AIAgents #DataPrivacy

Source: AI agent makers are promising privacy — will they deliver?

item.title: Meta Muse AI Agent Faces Multiple Security Vulnerabilities and Data Leaks
item.description:
Meta Muse AI Agent Faces Multiple Security Vulnerabilities and Data Leaks

Meta’s new consumer-facing AI agent, Muse, has encountered two security disclosures in a single week, including an exploit allowing account hijacking and a leak of its root filesystem.

🔍 Security Issues

  • Filesystem Leak: Peter James and Jonny L. Saunders independently coaxed Muse into sharing its entire root filesystem, including Ubuntu system files, internal documentation, and app templates. Saunders noted that Muse had “Almost no prompt injection resistance.”
  • Account Hijacking: Security researcher Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allows attackers to hijack the AI agent, redirect transcription processing, and gain complete control of a user’s Muse account. Meta issued a hotfix for this issue.

🧩 How it Works

  • Infrastructure: Muse runs in persistent Linux virtual machines for each user. Zuckerberg stated these are “isolated linux computer[s] with a browser, CPU, memory, and storage.”
  • Data Handling: The agent stores its memory in plain Markdown files and performs a nightly “dream” review of recent conversations to create guidance for future interactions.
  • Capabilities: Many capabilities are hard-coded, such as the ability to cancel subscriptions and the “machinery that manages runaway agent spawning.”
  • Integrations: James found references to “Meta Home Link,” which appears to provide Muse access to devices on a home network.

⚙️ Key Details

Researchers James and Saunders gained access to JSON and Markdown files describing “Hatch” (the internal name for Muse), which detail how the system:

  • Processes requests
  • Handles data
  • Connects to services like Gmail

💡 Why it Matters

Meta representatives have responded to the filesystem leaks as follows:

Representative Perspective
Daniel Roberts (Spokesperson) Compared it to a laptop, stating “of course you can see the files” and that exporting VM data provides no privileged access to Meta infrastructure or other users’ data.
Nat Friedman (Superintelligence Labs) Tweeted that this was “intended behavior.”
David Singleton (Superintelligence Labs) Suggested users view Muse as a “free computer in the cloud” where they can do almost anything they could with a computer under their desk.

🚀 Availability

According to an Apptopia estimate, Muse has 600,000 daily active users in the US and topped the App Store charts shortly after its release.

#Meta #Muse #Cybersecurity #AIAgents #DataPrivacy

Source: Muse will apparently let you download its entire filesystem Source: Muse sure looks a lot like OpenClaw

item.title: Security Fix Addresses Table Permission Bypass Caused by Trailing Newlines
item.description:
Security Fix Addresses Table Permission Bypass Caused by Trailing Newlines

A security fix has been released to address a vulnerability that allowed requested table names to bypass standard permission controls. The issue centered on how specific character formatting could lead to the unauthorized exposure of data.

🔍 Overview

The update resolves a security flaw where a trailing newline included in a requested table name could bypass table permissions. This bypass allowed for the potential exposure of private rows that should have remained restricted.

⚙️ Key details

  • Vulnerability Type: Permission bypass via trailing newline in table names.
  • Impact: Exposure of private rows.
  • Reported by: dpfkdlemtp.
  • Reference ID: GHSA-h547-rmjf-5m2m.

#CyberSecurity #DataPrivacy #SoftwareSecurity #SecurityFix

Source: Release: datasette 0.65.5

item.title: Instruction-Driven PII Detector for Large Language Models
item.description:
Instruction-Driven PII Detector for Large Language Models

A new configurable, instruction-driven detector for Personally Identifiable Information (PII) has been released. The tool is designed to run on any large language model (LLM) managed on Amazon Bedrock or hosted on private infrastructure.

🔍 Overview

The detector treats the language model as a configurable and swappable component. It is evaluated on five public PII corpora across nine LLM-based detectors, including the OpenAI PrivacyFilter.

🧩 How it works

The detector is built from four components:

  • Prompt: Defines the schema in a single system-prompt template containing fifteen entity categories with one-line definitions, a do-not-flag list, and optional few-shot examples.
  • Backend: Runs the model via a uniform inference interface called the Inferencer.
  • Parsing-and-offset layer: Converts the model response into located spans.
  • Call sequence: A thin layer that ties the other components together.

Because LLMs cannot reliably produce character offsets, the model is instructed to respond with a JSON list containing the entity type and the exact text value found. A post-processing step then computes exact character offsets and removes duplicates.

⚙️ Key details

The detection logic resides entirely in the instructions and a thin parsing layer. This architecture provides several capabilities:

  • Configurability: The entity set can be changed via a one-line edit to the instructions without retraining or redeployment.
  • Multilingual Support: The system can reason about context across eight languages without requiring a translation step.
  • Deployment Flexibility: It can run on a managed API or inside a virtual private cloud (VPC).
Component Options/Details
Model Frontier Amazon Bedrock models or small open models on a single GPU
Managed Adapter Amazon Bedrock adapter (pii_detector/bedrock_inferencer.py)
Custom Adapter Open models (e.g., OSS-GPT 20B) served on own infrastructure with a GPU

🚀 Availability

The detector ships as the pii-detector package, available in the sample-llm-pii-detection repository. The full prompt is located in pii_detector/templates.py.

#LLM #PII #AmazonBedrock #DataPrivacy

Source: Model-agnostic PII detection with LLMs | Amazon Web Services
